OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol is rolling out worldwide in Microsoft Copilot, including Word, Excel and PowerPoint.
The heavier GPT-6.2 Astra goes to Copilot Cowork and Copilot Studio, and to the Office apps only for Frontier users.
Admins control who gets them.

paragraphs.text: Microsoft said on November 20, 2026 that OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol and GPT-6.2 Astra are joining the frontier models available in Microsoft Copilot. The announcement came in a post on the Microsoft Copilot Blog, which links to OpenAI's own launch page for the two models.

According to the post, GPT-6.2 Sol is rolling out worldwide to eligible users in Copilot Chat, Copilot Cowork, Copilot Studio, and Copilot in Excel, PowerPoint and Word. Startup Fortune, which reported the rollout on November 22, described Sol as the model most Copilot users will meet in everyday work.

GPT-6.2 Astra has a narrower rollout. Microsoft said it is reaching eligible users worldwide in Copilot Cowork and Copilot Studio. Users in Microsoft's Frontier program can also use Astra in Copilot Chat and in Copilot in Excel, PowerPoint and Word, the company said.

Microsoft said the models can handle work ranging from a first draft in Word to a multi-step task handed off to Copilot Cowork. It added that availability may vary by region and organization, and that administrators manage access through the Microsoft 365 admin center. The post did not give specific rollout dates and pointed readers to the Microsoft 365 roadmap and the Copilot release notes instead.
Both models are grounded in a customer's files, meetings, chats and business data through Work IQ, according to Microsoft, which said Work IQ operates within a user's existing permissions.

Microsoft's blog post did not mention pricing. Startup Fortune, citing Microsoft 365 Message Center notice MC1560916 as summarized by MWPro, reported that both models use usage-based billing in supported services and that Sol also comes with the Microsoft 365 Copilot user license.

The same report said broad use of Astra requires an administrator to turn on the OpenAI subprocessor setting, while OpenAI models that Microsoft runs through Azure OpenAI are not affected by that setting. Microsoft's blog post links to admin documentation for the subprocessor setting. Startup Fortune added that the notice rates the admin impact as high and tells IT teams to prepare support staff for usage limit messages.
Startup Fortune also reported API prices from a summary by Newmobilelife: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens for Sol, and $8 and $40 for Astra.
Microsoft's own models in the mix

The rollout follows the launch of Microsoft's own MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash models in GitHub Copilot three days earlier at Ignite, Startup Fortune noted. Microsoft claimed MAI Code 2 matches 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40 percent of the price, a figure based on its own benchmarks and on launch pricing that ends in May 2027, according to the report.
Startup Fortune also pointed to earlier coverage that OpenAI and Microsoft ended their exclusive partnership and revenue sharing arrangement on April 27, 2026.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the split is deliberate. Sol becomes the default upgrade that most licensed users get without anyone in IT doing much, while Astra, the heavier and more expensive model, sits behind an admin switch and metered billing. For a large company, the decision about which OpenAI model employees use is now as much a budget and policy setting as a product feature.

The next thing to watch is how many organizations turn on the OpenAI subprocessor setting for Astra, and whether usage limit messages become a common complaint as metered billing spreads through Copilot.
